source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/configs.rst; start_index: 0:
API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

RFModelConfig 
------

This is a core class in the RapidFire AI API that abstracts multiple Hugging Face APIs under the 
hood to simplify and unify all model-related specifications. In particular, it unifies model 
loading, training configurations, and LoRA settings into one class. 

It gives you flexibility to try out variations of LoRA adapter structures, training arguments for 
multiple control flows (SFT, DPO, and GRPO), formatting and metrics functions, and generation specifics. 

Some of the arguments (knobs) here can also be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued depending 
on its data type, as explained below. All this helps form the base set of knob combinations from which 
a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

API: Trainer Configs
===============

RapidFire AI's core APIs for trainer specifications are all thin wrappers around the 
corresponding APIs of Hugging Face's `TRL <https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/index>`__ libraries.


RFSFTConfig
------

This is a wrapper around :class:`SFTConfig` in HF TRL. 
The full signature and list of arguments are available on `this page 
<https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/sft_trainer#trl.SFTConfig>`__.

The only difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued 
or :class:`Range` valued in :class:`RFSFTConfig`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can be 
produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.
Other than the multi-config specification, this class preserves all semantics of Hugging Face's 
SFT trainer under the hood.

answer: RapidFire AI's adaptive execution engine differs from traditional sequential execution by sharding the dataset into chunks and processing all runs on one shard at a time, cycling through all shards. This allows for early insights into learning behaviors and eval metrics before the entire dataset is processed, reducing overhead and enabling dynamic real-time control over runs in flight. Traditional sequential execution processes each model config in full before moving to the next, leading to delayed insights and potential resource wastage.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 1977:
The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time 
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short. 

*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if 
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the 
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters 
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior. 
Under the hood, RapidFire AI automatically manages how runs and chunks are placed on GPUs, 
freeing you to focus fully on the logic of your AI experiment rather than wrestling with 
low-level systems issue to parallelize your work.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: -1:
.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu.png
   :width: 800px

In the above figure, all 3 model configs are shown for 1 epoch. RapidFire AI is set to use 4 chunks.
So, before model config 3 (M3) even starts in the sequential approach, RapidFire AI already shows you 
the learning behaviors of all 3 configs on the first 2-3 chunks. 
The overhead of swapping, represented by the thin gray box, is minimal, less than 5% of the runtime,
as per our measurements--thanks to our new efficient memory management techniques.

For inference evals for RAG/context engineering, such sharded execution means RapidFire AI surfaces eval metrics 
sooner based on a statistical technique known as *online aggregation* from the database systems literature.
Basically, see estimated values and confidence intervals for all eval metrics in real time as the shards 
get processed, ultimately converging to the exact metrics on the full dataset.


The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/experiment.rst; start_index: 0:
API: Experiment 
================

Overview
--------

An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation. 

Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts. 
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

The Experiment class has the functions and semantics detailed below. 
As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either :code:`"fit"` mode or :code:`"eval"` mode but not both. 
We plan to allow both modes in the same experiment very soon.

.. note::
  Only one function in this class can be run at a time. If you interrupt a long-running function, 
  say, :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()`, wait for up to 2min for the Python threads to be 
  cleaned up before running another function.


Experiment Constructor 
------

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/experiment.rst; start_index: 1743:
# Based on FiQA RAG chatbot tutorial notebook
	>>> experiment = Experiment(experiment_name="exp1-fiqa", mode="eval")
	Experiment exp1-fiqa created ...


**Notes:**

You can instantiate as many experiment objects as you want. 
We recommend explicitly ending a previous experiment (see :func:`end()` below) before starting 
a new one so that you are cognizant of your code and/or config changes across them.

If you are using Jupyter and if its kernel restarts or gets interrupted for whatever reason, you 
can just reconnect the kernel and pick up that experiment from where you left off by just rerunning 
its constructor cell as is (unless you ended the experiment explicitly). 
Using that object you can continue that experiment as before.




Run Fit
------

The main function to launch training (including LLM fine-tuning and post-training) and evaluation for a given config group in one go. 
See :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>` for more details on how to construct a config group.

RFGridSearch and RFRandomSearch differ in how they handle knob values as follows:

- RFGridSearch: The individual arguments (knobs) can be List valued or Range valued in an RFvLLMModelConfig. This allows specifying a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can be produced.

- RFRandomSearch: Each knob can have either a single value, or a List() of values, or a Range() of values. The semantics of sampling are independently-identically-distributed (IID), meaning we uniformly randomly pick a value from each discrete set and from each continuous set to construct the knob combination for one run. This process is repeated in an IID way to accumulate num_runs distinct combinations.

To set up RapidFire AI for RAG evaluation on a machine without GPUs, follow these steps:

1. Install dependencies and the RapidFire AI package:
   - Ensure Python 3.12+ is installed.
   - Create and activate a virtual environment.
   - Install RapidFire AI using pip.

2. Initialize RapidFire AI for RAG evaluation:
   - Run the command `rapidfireai init --evals` to install specific dependencies and initialize RapidFire AI for RAG evals.

3. Start RapidFire AI services:
   - Run the command `rapidfireai start` to start the frontend with the ML metrics dashboard and the API server.
   - Ensure the start is successful with "Available endpoints" printed before proceeding.

4. Provide a valid OpenAI API key via a config argument, as you will be using OpenAI APIs instead of self-hosted models.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/icops.rst; start_index: 3976:
IC ops can be invoked as intermittently as you want during a long-running :func:`run_fit()`. 
So, you can launch, say, 16 configs in one go (even on a 4-GPU machine), check in after a few chunks,  
and stop bottom 80% of the runs. You can let the top performers continue for longer. Then you can 
clone and modify some to add new finer grained runs and warm start their parameters. And so on.

Under the hood, RapidFire AI automatically adjusts the apportioning of the GPUs among all ongoing 
runs to ensure maximal GPU utilization.




Stop
----

This IC Op earmarks a run to be stopped at the end of its current chunk. 
It will still be alive but it will not use any GPU resources from the next chunk. 
You will still see its minibatch-level plots advancing for the current chunk. 
You cannot stop an already stopped or deleted run.

The preprocess_fn function in the run_evals pipeline is a mandatory user-provided function that prepares the inputs for the generator model. It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process before generation. The system injects the following arguments into this function:

- batch: A dictionary with a batch of examples, with dataset field names as keys and lists as values.
- rag: An instance of RFLangChainRagSpec.
- prompt_manager: An instance of RFPromptManager.

The function signature is:
.. py:function:: preprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list], rag: RFLangChainRagSpec, prompt_manager: RFPromptManager) -> dict[str, list]

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/evalsfunctions.rst; start_index: 0:
API: User-Provided Functions for Run Evals
===============

Users can provide the following custom functions as part of their eval config to be used in :func:`run_evals()`.
Note that each leaf config can have its own set of functions for all of these.


Preprocess Function
-------------------

Mandatory user-provided function to prepare the inputs to be given to the generator model. 
It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process before generation.
Pass it directly to the :code:`preprocess_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.

The system injects into this function the batch data, as well as the RAG spec and 
the prompt manager of an individual leaf config.


.. py:function:: preprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list], rag: RFLangChainRagSpec, prompt_manager: RFPromptManager) -> dict[str, list]

   :param batch: Dictionary with a batch of examples with dataset field names as keys and lists as values
   :type batch: dict[str, list]

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/evalsfunctions.rst; start_index: 7037:
Postprocess Function
--------------------

Optional user-provided function to postprocess a batch of examples and their respective generated outputs, 
which is injected into this function by the system. 
This is useful for, say, extracting structured information from generations, adding ground truth data, 
or performing any transformations needed before computing metrics.

It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process after generation and before metric computation.
Pass it directly to the :code:`postprocess_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.


.. py:function:: postprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list]) -> dict[str, list]

   :param batch: Dictionary containing a batch of examples, including their respective generated outputs under the reserved key :code:`"generated_text"`.
   :type batch: dict[str, list]

   :return: Dictionary containing the postprocessed batch with any new or modified keys
   :rtype: dict[str, list]

External Vector Stores: Pinecone and PGVector
-------

RapidFire AI also supports external persistent vector stores beyond the default in-memory FAISS.
This allows you to scale to larger corpora, persist indexes across runs and experiments, and leverage managed vector DBMS services.
As of this writing, **Pinecone** (hosted serverless or pod-based) and **PostgreSQL PGVector** (self-hosted or managed) are supported.

Each external store supports three modes of operation:

- **Create mode:** Build a new index from base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG.
- **Read mode:** Retrieve from a pre-existing index and use it for RAG. 
- **Update mode:** Add new content to an existing index from additional base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG. 

See the :doc:`API: LangChain RAG Spec page</ragspecs>` for more details on how to specify these external vector stores.

------------

Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time 
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short. 

*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if 
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the 
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters 
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior.

freeing you to focus fully on the logic of your AI experiment rather than wrestling with 
low-level systems issue to parallelize your work.

answer: Online aggregation in the context of RapidFire AI evals is a statistical technique that allows you to see estimated values and confidence intervals for all eval metrics in real time as the shards get processed, ultimately converging to the exact metrics on the full dataset. It supports three confidence interval strategies: "normal", "bootstrap", and "t". These strategies can be specified under the key "online_strategy_kwargs" in your config dictionary, along with the confidence level (recommended 95%) and whether to perform "finite population correction" (FPC) or not.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: -1:
Confidence Intervals
--------------------

The data points in the evals dataset are **assigned to shards uniformly randomly**, i.e., 
RapidFire AI performs sampling without replacement. 
Based on that, it supports 3 strategies to calculate confidence intervals for projected estimates of metrics. 
You can indicate the confidence level (we recommend 95%) and whether to perform "finite population correction" (FPC) or not. 
These values can be specified under the key :code:`"online_strategy_kwargs"` in your config dictionary as illustrated below.

.. code-block:: python

    # Based on FiQA RAG tutorial use case
    "online_strategy_kwargs": {
        "strategy_name": "normal",
        "confidence_level": 0.95,
        "use_fpc": True,
    },

Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and

their **incrementally computed** eval metrics shown in real time with confidence intervals.

One clone is then stopped halfway through the aggregation, while the other two run to completion.

API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs.

knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

Overview
--------

An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation. 

Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts. 
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

The Experiment class has the functions and semantics detailed below. 
As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either :code:`"fit"` mode or :code:`"eval"` mode but not both. 
We plan to allow both modes in the same experiment very soon.

.. note::
  Only one function in this class can be run at a time. If you interrupt a long-running function, 
  say, :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()`, wait for up to 2min for the Python threads to be 
  cleaned up before running another function.

Dashboard: Interactive Control (IC) Ops
===============

Interactive Control Operations (IC Ops) are a powerful differentiating aspect of RapidFire AI 
that enable *rapid experimentation* capability for AI customization. 


Motivation for IC Ops
----

IC Ops are control operations over the runs *in flight* in an ongoing experiment. 
They are motivated by an often under-appreciated pain point felt by many AI developers: 

* How accurate a given configuration will be is *impossible* to tell upfront in general. Experimentation is critical: one must try alternate configs based on their intuition about their specific use case, dataset, model, and eval metrics.

* Not all configs are made equal. One must be able to easily try and retry values, zoom into promising regions of values, adjust on the fly, etc. This can help reach better eval metrics/model alignment more quickly. Otherwise, one might squander their (labeled) data and/or waste resources.

As of this writing, we support 4 IC Ops: **Stop**, **Resume**, **Clone-Modify**, and **Delete**. 
We explain each shortly below.

All IC Ops on a run are queued by the system and **executed at a chunk boundary** for that run. 
This avoids potentially non-deterministic or other inconsistent behaviors during concurrent run execution.
Note that different runs might reach their chunk boundary at different points in time.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

External Vector Stores: Pinecone and PGVector
-------

RapidFire AI also supports external persistent vector stores beyond the default in-memory FAISS.
This allows you to scale to larger corpora, persist indexes across runs and experiments, and leverage managed vector DBMS services.
As of this writing, **Pinecone** (hosted serverless or pod-based) and **PostgreSQL PGVector** (self-hosted or managed) are supported.

Each external store supports three modes of operation:

- **Create mode:** Build a new index from base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG.
- **Read mode:** Retrieve from a pre-existing index and use it for RAG. 
- **Update mode:** Add new content to an existing index from additional base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG. 

See the :doc:`API: LangChain RAG Spec page</ragspecs>` for more details on how to specify these external vector stores.

answer: Online aggregation in the context of RapidFire AI evals is an approach that assigns data points in the evals dataset to shards uniformly randomly, performing sampling without replacement. It supports three confidence interval strategies: "normal", "t", and "bootstrap". These strategies can be specified under the key "online_strategy_kwargs" in the config dictionary, along with the confidence level (e.g., 0.95) and whether to perform "finite population correction" (FPC) or not.

Confidence Intervals
--------------------

The data points in the evals dataset are **assigned to shards uniformly randomly**, i.e., 
RapidFire AI performs sampling without replacement. 
Based on that, it supports 3 strategies to calculate confidence intervals for projected estimates of metrics. 
You can indicate the confidence level (we recommend 95%) and whether to perform "finite population correction" (FPC) or not. 
These values can be specified under the key :code:`"online_strategy_kwargs"` in your config dictionary as illustrated below.

.. code-block:: python

    # Based on FiQA RAG tutorial use case
    "online_strategy_kwargs": {
        "strategy_name": "normal",
        "confidence_level": 0.95,
        "use_fpc": True,
    },

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process.

API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

answer: RapidFire AI's adaptive execution engine differs from traditional sequential execution by sharding the dataset into chunks and processing multiple configurations in parallel, one shard at a time, rather than waiting for a run to see the whole dataset. This approach allows for interruptible execution, dynamic real-time control over runs, and earlier visibility into learning behaviors and evaluation metrics through online aggregation. The overhead of swapping chunks is minimal, less than 5% of the runtime.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time 
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short. 

*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if 
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the 
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters 
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior. 
Under the hood, RapidFire AI automatically manages how runs and chunks are placed on GPUs, 
freeing you to focus fully on the logic of your AI experiment rather than wrestling with 
low-level systems issue to parallelize your work.

API: Experiment 
================

Overview
--------

An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation. 

Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts. 
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

The Experiment class has the functions and semantics detailed below. 
As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either :code:`"fit"` mode or :code:`"eval"` mode but not both. 
We plan to allow both modes in the same experiment very soon.

.. note::
  Only one function in this class can be run at a time. If you interrupt a long-running function, 
  say, :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()`, wait for up to 2min for the Python threads to be 
  cleaned up before running another function.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/rag_fiqa.rst; start_index: -1:
External Vector Stores: Pinecone and PGVector
-------

RapidFire AI also supports external persistent vector stores beyond the default in-memory FAISS.
This allows you to scale to larger corpora, persist indexes across runs and experiments, and leverage managed vector DBMS services.
As of this writing, **Pinecone** (hosted serverless or pod-based) and **PostgreSQL PGVector** (self-hosted or managed) are supported.

Each external store supports three modes of operation:

- **Create mode:** Build a new index from base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG.
- **Read mode:** Retrieve from a pre-existing index and use it for RAG. 
- **Update mode:** Add new content to an existing index from additional base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG. 

See the :doc:`API: LangChain RAG Spec page</ragspecs>` for more details on how to specify these external vector stores.

The FiQA RAG tutorial notebooks have also been extended to showcase the external stores as below:

answer: Online aggregation in RapidFire AI evals is a statistical technique that provides running metric estimates with confidence intervals in real time as shards of data are processed. It supports three confidence interval strategies: normal, t, and binomial. These strategies can be configured with a confidence level (e.g., 95%) and an option for finite population correction (FPC) under the key "online_strategy_kwargs" in the config dictionary.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: -1:
Confidence Intervals
--------------------

The data points in the evals dataset are **assigned to shards uniformly randomly**, i.e., 
RapidFire AI performs sampling without replacement. 
Based on that, it supports 3 strategies to calculate confidence intervals for projected estimates of metrics. 
You can indicate the confidence level (we recommend 95%) and whether to perform "finite population correction" (FPC) or not. 
These values can be specified under the key :code:`"online_strategy_kwargs"` in your config dictionary as illustrated below.

.. code-block:: python

    # Based on FiQA RAG tutorial use case
    "online_strategy_kwargs": {
        "strategy_name": "normal",
        "confidence_level": 0.95,
        "use_fpc": True,
    },

while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in 
conjunction for even lower runtimes/costs.


Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process.

you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and

API: Experiment 
================

Overview
--------

An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation. 

Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts. 
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

The Experiment class has the functions and semantics detailed below. 
As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either :code:`"fit"` mode or :code:`"eval"` mode but not both. 
We plan to allow both modes in the same experiment very soon.

.. note::
  Only one function in this class can be run at a time. If you interrupt a long-running function, 
  say, :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()`, wait for up to 2min for the Python threads to be 
  cleaned up before running another function.


Experiment Constructor 
------

answer:

- mode (str, optional): Mode of this experiment, either "fit" or "eval"; default is "fit"
- experiments_path (str, optional): Path to a folder to store this experiment's artifacts. Default is "./rapidfire_experiments"

External Vector Stores: Pinecone and PGVector
-------

RapidFire AI also supports external persistent vector stores beyond the default in-memory FAISS.
This allows you to scale to larger corpora, persist indexes across runs and experiments, and leverage managed vector DBMS services.
As of this writing, **Pinecone** (hosted serverless or pod-based) and **PostgreSQL PGVector** (self-hosted or managed) are supported.

Each external store supports three modes of operation:

- **Create mode:** Build a new index from base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG.
- **Read mode:** Retrieve from a pre-existing index and use it for RAG. 
- **Update mode:** Add new content to an existing index from additional base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG. 

See the :doc:`API: LangChain RAG Spec page</ragspecs>` for more details on how to specify these external vector stores.

answer: Online aggregation in the context of RapidFire AI evals is a method where data points in the evals dataset are assigned to shards uniformly randomly, and eval metrics are incrementally computed in real time with confidence intervals. It supports three confidence interval strategies: "normal", "t", and "bootstrap". These strategies can be specified under the key "online_strategy_kwargs" in the config dictionary, along with the confidence level (e.g., 0.95) and whether to perform finite population correction (FPC) or not.

Confidence Intervals
--------------------

The data points in the evals dataset are **assigned to shards uniformly randomly**, i.e., 
RapidFire AI performs sampling without replacement. 
Based on that, it supports 3 strategies to calculate confidence intervals for projected estimates of metrics. 
You can indicate the confidence level (we recommend 95%) and whether to perform "finite population correction" (FPC) or not. 
These values can be specified under the key :code:`"online_strategy_kwargs"` in your config dictionary as illustrated below.

.. code-block:: python

    # Based on FiQA RAG tutorial use case
    "online_strategy_kwargs": {
        "strategy_name": "normal",
        "confidence_level": 0.95,
        "use_fpc": True,
    },

API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

------

This is a core class in the RapidFire AI API that abstracts multiple Hugging Face APIs under the 
hood to simplify and unify all model-related specifications. In particular, it unifies model 
loading, training configurations, and LoRA settings into one class. 

It gives you flexibility to try out variations of LoRA adapter structures, training arguments for 
multiple control flows (SFT, DPO, and GRPO), formatting and metrics functions, and generation specifics. 

Some of the arguments (knobs) here can also be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued depending 
on its data type, as explained below. All this helps form the base set of knob combinations from which 
a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

knob combination for one run. 
Then we repeat that sampling process in an IID way to accumulate :code:`num_runs` distinct combinations.

===============

RapidFire AI's core APIs for trainer specifications are all thin wrappers around the 
corresponding APIs of Hugging Face's `TRL <https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/index>`__ libraries.

The full signature and list of arguments are available on `this page

The only difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued 
or :class:`Range` valued in :class:`RFSFTConfig`.

SFT trainer under the hood.

answer: RapidFire AI's adaptive execution engine differs from traditional sequential execution by sharding the dataset into chunks and processing all runs on one shard at a time, cycling through all shards. This allows for early insights into learning behaviors and eval metrics before the entire dataset is processed. The engine also enables dynamic real-time control over runs, including stopping, resuming, cloning, and modifying configurations, with minimal overhead for swapping. Traditional sequential execution processes each model configuration fully before moving to the next, leading to delayed insights and potential resource wastage.

What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time 
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short. 

*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if 
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the 
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters 
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior. 
Under the hood, RapidFire AI automatically manages how runs and chunks are placed on GPUs, 
freeing you to focus fully on the logic of your AI experiment rather than wrestling with 
low-level systems issue to parallelize your work.

.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu.png
   :width: 800px

In the above figure, all 3 model configs are shown for 1 epoch. RapidFire AI is set to use 4 chunks.
So, before model config 3 (M3) even starts in the sequential approach, RapidFire AI already shows you 
the learning behaviors of all 3 configs on the first 2-3 chunks. 
The overhead of swapping, represented by the thin gray box, is minimal, less than 5% of the runtime,
as per our measurements--thanks to our new efficient memory management techniques.

For inference evals for RAG/context engineering, such sharded execution means RapidFire AI surfaces eval metrics 
sooner based on a statistical technique known as *online aggregation* from the database systems literature.
Basically, see estimated values and confidence intervals for all eval metrics in real time as the shards 
get processed, ultimately converging to the exact metrics on the full dataset.


The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/configs.rst; start_index: 0:
API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/trainers.rst; start_index: 0:
API: Trainer Configs
===============

RapidFire AI's core APIs for trainer specifications are all thin wrappers around the 
corresponding APIs of Hugging Face's `TRL <https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/index>`__ libraries.


RFSFTConfig
------

This is a wrapper around :class:`SFTConfig` in HF TRL. 
The full signature and list of arguments are available on `this page 
<https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/sft_trainer#trl.SFTConfig>`__.

The only difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued 
or :class:`Range` valued in :class:`RFSFTConfig`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can be 
produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.
Other than the multi-config specification, this class preserves all semantics of Hugging Face's 
SFT trainer under the hood.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/models.rst; start_index: 2950:
RFModelConfig 
------

This is a core class in the RapidFire AI API that abstracts multiple Hugging Face APIs under the 
hood to simplify and unify all model-related specifications. In particular, it unifies model 
loading, training configurations, and LoRA settings into one class. 

It gives you flexibility to try out variations of LoRA adapter structures, training arguments for 
multiple control flows (SFT, DPO, and GRPO), formatting and metrics functions, and generation specifics. 

Some of the arguments (knobs) here can also be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued depending 
on its data type, as explained below. All this helps form the base set of knob combinations from which 
a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.


.. py:class:: RFModelConfig

For :func:`RFRandomSearch()`, each knob can have either a single value, or a :func:`List()` of values, or a 
 :func:`Range()` of values. The semantics of sampling are independently-identically-distributed (IID), i.e.,
we uniformly randomly pick a value from each discrete set and from each continuous set to construct the 
knob combination for one run. 
Then we repeat that sampling process in an IID way to accumulate :code:`num_runs` distinct combinations.

Note that the return types of the config group generators are internal to RapidFire AI and they are usable only 
within the context of :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()` in the :class:`Experiment` class.

API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

Config Group
-----

A set of config dictionary instances, produced in bulk by providing a config dictionary 
with set-valued knobs to a config-group generator method (see below). 
It can also be a Python list of individual config dictionaries or config-group generators recursively.

Read more here: :doc:`API: Multi-Config Specification</configs>`.


Config Group Generator
-----

A method to generate a group of config dictionaries in one go based on an input
config dictionary with set-valued knobs (:class:`List` or :class:`Range`). 
Currently supported generator methods are grid search (:class:`RFGridSearch`) and 
random search (:class:`RFRandomSearch`). Support for AutoML heuristics coming soon. 

Read more here: :doc:`API: Multi-Config Specification</configs>`.

answer: RapidFire AI's adaptive execution engine differs from traditional sequential execution by sharding the dataset into chunks and scheduling runs on one shard at a time, cycling through all shards. This allows for interruptible execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs, dynamic experiment control (stop, resume, clone-modify), and avoids the need for manual checkpoint management. Traditional sequential execution waits for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs or full eval metrics calculation.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 4884:
A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong 
conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone LLMs/DL models. It requires manual checkpoint 
management, adding tedious file work. You also do not get dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify),
or you must reimplement such tricky operations, taking time away from your AI application work.

RapidFire AI takes such practical heuristics to their logical conclusion with shard-based 
adaptive multi-config execution with dynamic experiment control. This offers you maximum power 
and flexibility for AI development without extra DevOps grunt work, i.e., *rapid experimentation*.

The above said, note that downsampling is *complementary* to rapid experimentation--feel free 
do both! The adaptive execution can operate on your downsampled dataset all the same.

API: Experiment 
================

Overview
--------

An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation. 

Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts. 
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

The Experiment class has the functions and semantics detailed below. 
As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either :code:`"fit"` mode or :code:`"eval"` mode but not both. 
We plan to allow both modes in the same experiment very soon.

.. note::
  Only one function in this class can be run at a time. If you interrupt a long-running function, 
  say, :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()`, wait for up to 2min for the Python threads to be 
  cleaned up before running another function.


Experiment Constructor 
------

Glossary of Key Terms and Concepts
==========


Artifacts
-----
All files related to an experiment saved under in a local folder with its path specified by
:code:`experiments_path` in the experiment's constructor.
Includes the final (and possibly all epoch-level) model checkpoints of all runs across 
all :func:`run_fit()` in that experiment, and all associated metrics files.

Read more here: :doc:`API: Experiment</experiment>`.


Config Dictionary
-----

A dictionary of key-value pairs that specify a full model training configuration. 
A knob's value can be a singleton or set-valued (:class:`List` or :class:`Range`). 
A dictionary with set-valued knobs be fed to a config-group generator method. 
A single combination of knob values in this dictionary is called a "leaf" config. 
RapidFire AI instantiates one run per leaf config, and its values are injected via the 
:code:`model_config` argument to your :func:`create_model_fn()` function.

Dashboard: Interactive Control (IC) Ops
===============

Interactive Control Operations (IC Ops) are a powerful differentiating aspect of RapidFire AI 
that enable *rapid experimentation* capability for AI customization. 


Motivation for IC Ops
----

IC Ops are control operations over the runs *in flight* in an ongoing experiment. 
They are motivated by an often under-appreciated pain point felt by many AI developers: 

* How accurate a given configuration will be is *impossible* to tell upfront in general. Experimentation is critical: one must try alternate configs based on their intuition about their specific use case, dataset, model, and eval metrics.

* Not all configs are made equal. One must be able to easily try and retry values, zoom into promising regions of values, adjust on the fly, etc. This can help reach better eval metrics/model alignment more quickly. Otherwise, one might squander their (labeled) data and/or waste resources.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 1977:
The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time 
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short. 

*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if 
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the 
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters 
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior. 
Under the hood, RapidFire AI automatically manages how runs and chunks are placed on GPUs, 
freeing you to focus fully on the logic of your AI experiment rather than wrestling with 
low-level systems issue to parallelize your work.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/rag_fiqa.rst; start_index: -1:
External Vector Stores: Pinecone and PGVector
-------

RapidFire AI also supports external persistent vector stores beyond the default in-memory FAISS.
This allows you to scale to larger corpora, persist indexes across runs and experiments, and leverage managed vector DBMS services.
As of this writing, **Pinecone** (hosted serverless or pod-based) and **PostgreSQL PGVector** (self-hosted or managed) are supported.

Each external store supports three modes of operation:

- **Create mode:** Build a new index from base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG.
- **Read mode:** Retrieve from a pre-existing index and use it for RAG. 
- **Update mode:** Add new content to an existing index from additional base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG. 

See the :doc:`API: LangChain RAG Spec page</ragspecs>` for more details on how to specify these external vector stores.

The FiQA RAG tutorial notebooks have also been extended to showcase the external stores as below:

answer: Online aggregation in the context of RapidFire AI evals is an approach that adapts the idea from database systems research to LLM evals, allowing for real-time evaluation metrics and confidence intervals as data shards are processed. It supports three confidence interval strategies: normal, t-distribution, and bootstrap. These strategies can be specified under the key "online_strategy_kwargs" in the config dictionary, along with parameters like "confidence_level" (recommended 95%) and "use_fpc" (finite population correction).

Confidence Intervals
--------------------

The data points in the evals dataset are **assigned to shards uniformly randomly**, i.e., 
RapidFire AI performs sampling without replacement. 
Based on that, it supports 3 strategies to calculate confidence intervals for projected estimates of metrics. 
You can indicate the confidence level (we recommend 95%) and whether to perform "finite population correction" (FPC) or not. 
These values can be specified under the key :code:`"online_strategy_kwargs"` in your config dictionary as illustrated below.

.. code-block:: python

    # Based on FiQA RAG tutorial use case
    "online_strategy_kwargs": {
        "strategy_name": "normal",
        "confidence_level": 0.95,
        "use_fpc": True,
    },

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: -1:
.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu.png
   :width: 800px

In the above figure, all 3 model configs are shown for 1 epoch. RapidFire AI is set to use 4 chunks.
So, before model config 3 (M3) even starts in the sequential approach, RapidFire AI already shows you 
the learning behaviors of all 3 configs on the first 2-3 chunks. 
The overhead of swapping, represented by the thin gray box, is minimal, less than 5% of the runtime,
as per our measurements--thanks to our new efficient memory management techniques.

For inference evals for RAG/context engineering, such sharded execution means RapidFire AI surfaces eval metrics 
sooner based on a statistical technique known as *online aggregation* from the database systems literature.
Basically, see estimated values and confidence intervals for all eval metrics in real time as the shards 
get processed, ultimately converging to the exact metrics on the full dataset.


The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

answer: RapidFire AI's adaptive execution engine differs from traditional sequential execution by sharding the dataset into chunks and scheduling runs on one shard at a time, cycling through all shards. This allows for interruptible execution across GPUs/CPUs, dynamic experiment control (stop, resume, clone-modify), and avoids the need for manual checkpoint management. Traditional sequential execution waits for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs or full eval metrics calculation.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 4884:
A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong 
conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone LLMs/DL models. It requires manual checkpoint 
management, adding tedious file work. You also do not get dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify),
or you must reimplement such tricky operations, taking time away from your AI application work.

RapidFire AI takes such practical heuristics to their logical conclusion with shard-based 
adaptive multi-config execution with dynamic experiment control. This offers you maximum power 
and flexibility for AI development without extra DevOps grunt work, i.e., *rapid experimentation*.

The above said, note that downsampling is *complementary* to rapid experimentation--feel free 
do both! The adaptive execution can operate on your downsampled dataset all the same.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/overview.rst; start_index: 0:
Overview of RapidFire AI Package
==============

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms your LLM pipeline customization 
from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, 
dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization.

For *RAG and context engineering evals*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: RAG and Context Engineering</walkthroughrag>`.

For *SFT and RFT/post-training workflows*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: SFT/RFT</walkthroughft>`.


RapidFire AI is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between the IDE
where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend.

.. image:: /images/rf-usage.png
   :width: 800px

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/configs.rst; start_index: 0:
API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

To set up RapidFire AI for RAG evaluation on a machine without GPUs, follow these steps:

1. Install RapidFire AI using pip:
   ```
   pip install rapidfireai
   ```

2. Verify the installation:
   ```
   rapidfireai --version
   ```

3. Uninstall hf-xet (due to a known issue):
   ```
   pip uninstall -y hf-xet
   ```

4. Initialize RapidFire AI for RAG evaluations:
   ```
   rapidfireai init --evals
   ```

This setup does not require GPUs and can be done on any local machine or cloud machine.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

API: LangChain RAG Spec
===============

RapidFire AI's core API for defining the stages of a RAG pipeline before the generator is a wrapper around the corresponding APIs of LangChain.
In particular, this class specifies all of the following stages: data loading, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, and reranking steps. 
Note that many of these stages are optional. 

Many of the arguments (knobs) here can also be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued depending 
on its data type, as explained below. All this forms the base set of knob combinations from which 
a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

Note that for plain prompt/context engineering use cases without RAG, you can skip providing this entire class.

The preprocess_fn function in the run_evals pipeline is a mandatory user-provided function that prepares the inputs to be given to the generator model. It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process before generation. The system injects the following arguments into this function:

- batch: A dictionary with a batch of examples with dataset field names as keys and lists as values.

- prompt_manager: An instance of RFPromptManager.

API: Generator Configs
===============

RapidFire AI supports both self-hosted open LLMs and closed model LLM APIs as the generator. 
As of this writing, it wraps around the model config of vLLM for the former and the OpenAI API for the latter. 
We plan to expand support for more generator plugins, including Gemini and Claude APIs, based on feedback. 


RFvLLMModelConfig
------

This is a wrapper around vLLM's :class:`config` and :class:`SamplingParams` classes. 
The full list of their arguments are available on `this page <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/api/vllm/config/index.html>`__ 
and `this page <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.6.4/dev/sampling_params.html>`__, respectively.

* **With Preprocessing:** This creates both Document Preprocessing workers and Query Processing workers. Provide :code:`document_loader`, optional :code:`text_splitter`, :code:`embedding_cfg`, and optional :code:`vector_store_cfg`. The document preprocessing workers operate on the base data, produce chunks (if :code:`text_splitter` provided), embed the chunks (or the whole documents if :code:`text_splitter` is skipped), and store them in the vector store. If :code:`vector_store_cfg` is not provided, RapidFire AI defaults to creating a FAISS flat vector store for you.

Online aggregation in the context of RapidFire AI evals is an approach that adapts the idea from database systems research to LLM evals, allowing for real-time metric estimates with confidence intervals. This enables users to stop poor configurations earlier, clone better configurations on the fly, and perform more informed exploration to achieve better eval metrics in less time.

The three confidence interval strategies supported are:
1. "normal"
2. "wilson"
3. "hoeffding"

Confidence Intervals
--------------------

The data points in the evals dataset are **assigned to shards uniformly randomly**, i.e., 
RapidFire AI performs sampling without replacement. 
Based on that, it supports 3 strategies to calculate confidence intervals for projected estimates of metrics. 
You can indicate the confidence level (we recommend 95%) and whether to perform "finite population correction" (FPC) or not. 
These values can be specified under the key :code:`"online_strategy_kwargs"` in your config dictionary as illustrated below.

.. code-block:: python

    # Based on FiQA RAG tutorial use case
    "online_strategy_kwargs": {
        "strategy_name": "normal",
        "confidence_level": 0.95,
        "use_fpc": True,
    },

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

Config Group
-----

A set of config dictionary instances, produced in bulk by providing a config dictionary 
with set-valued knobs to a config-group generator method (see below). 
It can also be a Python list of individual config dictionaries or config-group generators recursively.

Read more here: :doc:`API: Multi-Config Specification</configs>`.


Config Group Generator
-----

A method to generate a group of config dictionaries in one go based on an input
config dictionary with set-valued knobs (:class:`List` or :class:`Range`). 
Currently supported generator methods are grid search (:class:`RFGridSearch`) and 
random search (:class:`RFRandomSearch`). Support for AutoML heuristics coming soon. 

Read more here: :doc:`API: Multi-Config Specification</configs>`.



Experiment
------

This enables interruptible execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs and dynamic experiment control, offering maximum power and flexibility for AI development without extra DevOps work.

What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong 
conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone LLMs/DL models. It requires manual checkpoint 
management, adding tedious file work. You also do not get dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify),
or you must reimplement such tricky operations, taking time away from your AI application work.

RapidFire AI takes such practical heuristics to their logical conclusion with shard-based 
adaptive multi-config execution with dynamic experiment control. This offers you maximum power 
and flexibility for AI development without extra DevOps grunt work, i.e., *rapid experimentation*.

The above said, note that downsampling is *complementary* to rapid experimentation--feel free 
do both! The adaptive execution can operate on your downsampled dataset all the same.

API: Experiment 
================

Overview
--------

An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation. 

Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts. 
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

The Experiment class has the functions and semantics detailed below. 
As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either :code:`"fit"` mode or :code:`"eval"` mode but not both. 
We plan to allow both modes in the same experiment very soon.

.. note::
  Only one function in this class can be run at a time. If you interrupt a long-running function, 
  say, :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()`, wait for up to 2min for the Python threads to be 
  cleaned up before running another function.


Experiment Constructor 
------

Glossary of Key Terms and Concepts
==========


Artifacts
-----
All files related to an experiment saved under in a local folder with its path specified by
:code:`experiments_path` in the experiment's constructor.
Includes the final (and possibly all epoch-level) model checkpoints of all runs across 
all :func:`run_fit()` in that experiment, and all associated metrics files.

Read more here: :doc:`API: Experiment</experiment>`.


Config Dictionary
-----

A dictionary of key-value pairs that specify a full model training configuration. 
A knob's value can be a singleton or set-valued (:class:`List` or :class:`Range`). 
A dictionary with set-valued knobs be fed to a config-group generator method. 
A single combination of knob values in this dictionary is called a "leaf" config. 
RapidFire AI instantiates one run per leaf config, and its values are injected via the 
:code:`model_config` argument to your :func:`create_model_fn()` function.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/glossary.rst; start_index: -1:
Read more here: :doc:`API: Multi-Config Specification</configs>`.



Experiment
------

A core concept in the RapidFire AI API that defines a collection of training and evaluation 
operations performed. Each experiment is assigned a unique name that is used for both display 
of plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for artifact tracking. 
At any point in time, only one experiment can be alive. 

Read more here: :doc:`API: Experiment</experiment>`.


Experiment Ops
------

Computation methods associated with the :class:`Experiment` class of RapidFire AI: 
:func:`run_fit()`, :func:`end()`, and the constructor. 
Also includes two informational methods: :func:`get_runs_info()` and :func:`get_results()`. 
We will expand this API with more operations based on feedback, e.g., for batch testing 
and inference/generation.

Read more here: :doc:`API: Experiment</experiment>`.


Interactive Control Ops (IC Ops)
------

and launch them in one go.  
It can be a single config dictionary, a :code:`list` of config dictionaries, a config group generator output 
(:func:`RFGridSearch()` or :func:`RFRandomSearch()` for now), or even a :code:`list` with mix of configs or 
config group generator outputs as its elements.
Please see the :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</search>` for more details. 

Each individual config is passed as input to your :func:`create_model_fn()`. Inside it you can use whatever 
knob you set in the config group, e.g., model type or name to instantiate a model accordingly. 
You can import models from libraries such as HuggingFace transformers or load your own PyTorch checkpoints.

For :func:`RFRandomSearch()`, each knob can have either a single value, or a :func:`List()` of values, or a 
 :func:`Range()` of values. The semantics of sampling are independently-identically-distributed (IID), i.e.,
we uniformly randomly pick a value from each discrete set and from each continuous set to construct the 
knob combination for one run. 
Then we repeat that sampling process in an IID way to accumulate :code:`num_runs` distinct combinations.

Note that the return types of the config group generators are internal to RapidFire AI and they are usable only 
within the context of :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()` in the :class:`Experiment` class.

The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time 
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short. 

*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if 
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the 
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters 
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior. 
Under the hood, RapidFire AI automatically manages how runs and chunks are placed on GPUs, 
freeing you to focus fully on the logic of your AI experiment rather than wrestling with 
low-level systems issue to parallelize your work.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/icops.rst; start_index: 0:
Dashboard: Interactive Control (IC) Ops
===============

Interactive Control Operations (IC Ops) are a powerful differentiating aspect of RapidFire AI 
that enable *rapid experimentation* capability for AI customization. 


Motivation for IC Ops
----

IC Ops are control operations over the runs *in flight* in an ongoing experiment. 
They are motivated by an often under-appreciated pain point felt by many AI developers: 

* How accurate a given configuration will be is *impossible* to tell upfront in general. Experimentation is critical: one must try alternate configs based on their intuition about their specific use case, dataset, model, and eval metrics.

* Not all configs are made equal. One must be able to easily try and retry values, zoom into promising regions of values, adjust on the fly, etc. This can help reach better eval metrics/model alignment more quickly. Otherwise, one might squander their (labeled) data and/or waste resources.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/rag_fiqa.rst; start_index: -1:
External Vector Stores: Pinecone and PGVector
-------

RapidFire AI also supports external persistent vector stores beyond the default in-memory FAISS.
This allows you to scale to larger corpora, persist indexes across runs and experiments, and leverage managed vector DBMS services.
As of this writing, **Pinecone** (hosted serverless or pod-based) and **PostgreSQL PGVector** (self-hosted or managed) are supported.

Each external store supports three modes of operation:

- **Create mode:** Build a new index from base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG.
- **Read mode:** Retrieve from a pre-existing index and use it for RAG. 
- **Update mode:** Add new content to an existing index from additional base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG. 

See the :doc:`API: LangChain RAG Spec page</ragspecs>` for more details on how to specify these external vector stores.

The FiQA RAG tutorial notebooks have also been extended to showcase the external stores as below:

API: LangChain RAG Spec
===============

RapidFire AI's core API for defining the stages of a RAG pipeline before the generator is a wrapper around the corresponding APIs of LangChain.
In particular, this class specifies all of the following stages: data loading, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, and reranking steps. 
Note that many of these stages are optional. 

Many of the arguments (knobs) here can also be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued depending 
on its data type, as explained below. All this forms the base set of knob combinations from which 
a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

Note that for plain prompt/context engineering use cases without RAG, you can skip providing this entire class. 
If you'd like to do few-shot prompting instead, also read :doc:`API: Prompt Manager and Other Eval Config Knobs page</promptothers>`.
Here is an illustration of the non-RAG prompt engineering workflow, with optional few-shot prompting.

The data points in the evals dataset are **assigned to shards uniformly randomly**, i.e.,
