Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

ImportError in between Experiments
------

If you run multiple experiments back to back from the same notebook/IDE session, you might 
see the following error appear occasionally: 

.. code-block:: python

   ImportError: cannot import name 'GenerationMixin' from 'transformers.generation'

If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:

* Run the command :code:`ps - ef | grep python`, look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes, and kill if there are any with command :code:`kill -9 [PID]`.

* Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill as above.

* Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

RFModelConfig 
------

This is a core class in the RapidFire AI API that abstracts multiple Hugging Face APIs under the 
hood to simplify and unify all model-related specifications. In particular, it unifies model 
loading, training configurations, and LoRA settings into one class. 

It gives you flexibility to try out variations of LoRA adapter structures, training arguments for 
multiple control flows (SFT, DPO, and GRPO), formatting and metrics functions, and generation specifics. 

Some of the arguments (knobs) here can also be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued depending 
on its data type, as explained below. All this helps form the base set of knob combinations from which 
a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/glossary.rst; start_index: 0:
Glossary of Key Terms and Concepts
==========


Artifacts
-----
All files related to an experiment saved under in a local folder with its path specified by
:code:`experiments_path` in the experiment's constructor.
Includes the final (and possibly all epoch-level) model checkpoints of all runs across 
all :func:`run_fit()` in that experiment, and all associated metrics files.

Read more here: :doc:`API: Experiment</experiment>`.


Config Dictionary
-----

A dictionary of key-value pairs that specify a full model training configuration. 
A knob's value can be a singleton or set-valued (:class:`List` or :class:`Range`). 
A dictionary with set-valued knobs be fed to a config-group generator method. 
A single combination of knob values in this dictionary is called a "leaf" config. 
RapidFire AI instantiates one run per leaf config, and its values are injected via the 
:code:`model_config` argument to your :func:`create_model_fn()` function.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/trainers.rst; start_index: 0:
API: Trainer Configs
===============

RapidFire AI's core APIs for trainer specifications are all thin wrappers around the 
corresponding APIs of Hugging Face's `TRL <https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/index>`__ libraries.


RFSFTConfig
------

This is a wrapper around :class:`SFTConfig` in HF TRL. 
The full signature and list of arguments are available on `this page 
<https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/sft_trainer#trl.SFTConfig>`__.

The only difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued 
or :class:`Range` valued in :class:`RFSFTConfig`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can be 
produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.
Other than the multi-config specification, this class preserves all semantics of Hugging Face's 
SFT trainer under the hood.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/configs.rst; start_index: 0:
API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

------

This is a core class in the RapidFire AI API that abstracts multiple Hugging Face APIs under the 
hood to simplify and unify all model-related specifications. In particular, it unifies model 
loading, training configurations, and LoRA settings into one class. 

It gives you flexibility to try out variations of LoRA adapter structures, training arguments for 
multiple control flows (SFT, DPO, and GRPO), formatting and metrics functions, and generation specifics. 

Some of the arguments (knobs) here can also be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued depending 
on its data type, as explained below. All this helps form the base set of knob combinations from which 
a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.


.. py:class:: RFModelConfig

1. Install dependencies and package:
   - Ensure Python 3.12+ is installed.
   - Create and activate a virtual environment.
   - Install RapidFire AI using pip.
   - Verify the installation by checking the version.

   ```bash
   python3 --version  # must be 3.12.x
   python3 -m venv .venv
   source .venv/bin/activate
   pip install rapidfireai
   rapidfireai --version
   ```

2. Initialize and start RapidFire AI server:
   - Run the initialization command to set up dependencies for fine-tuning workflows.

   ```bash
   rapidfireai init
   ```

3. To access gated Hugging Face models:
   - Provide your Hugging Face account token. This can be done by setting the token in your environment or configuration.

To start the RapidFire AI services:
   - Run the start command to launch the frontend and API server.

   ```bash
   rapidfireai start
   ```

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

	:param dataset: Evaluation dataset to measure eval metrics

answer:
RapidFire AI argues that simply downsampling the evaluation data is insufficient compared to its online aggregation approach because:

1. Downsampling requires deciding a sample size upfront, which is challenging if evaluation metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence intervals can give false confidence in a sample.
2. Resampling manually adds manual work of juggling separate samples/files.
3. Downsampling alone does not offer the power of IC Ops and automated parallelization to try new configurations on the fly, which would require manual reimplementation.
4. A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone models. It also requires manual checkpoint management, adding tedious file work and lacking dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify).
5. RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach provides real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, allowing for more efficient comparison of configurations and data-driven decisions.

Why Not Just Downsample?
------------------------

One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here. 
:doc:`As also explained on this page</difference>`, downsampling alone has 
significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI. 

First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence 
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

RapidFire AI argues that simply downsampling the evaluation data is insufficient compared to its online aggregation approach because:

1. Downsampling requires deciding a sample size upfront, which is challenging with high variance in evaluation metrics.
2. Downsampling lacks confidence intervals, leading to potential false confidence in point estimates.
3. Downsampling does not provide the power of IC Ops and automated parallelization for dynamic configuration testing.
4. Downsampling introduces variance from a static snapshot, risking incorrect conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone models.
5. Downsampling requires manual checkpoint management and lacks dynamic control features like stop, resume, and clone-modify.
6. RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach offers real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, enabling more efficient configuration comparisons and data-driven decisions.

==============

   :width: 800px

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

RapidFire AI argues that simply downsampling the evaluation data is insufficient because:

1. Downsampling introduces variance from a static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone models.
2. It requires manual checkpoint management, adding tedious file work.
3. It does not offer dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify) without reimplementation.
4. Downsampling alone does not provide the power of IC Ops and automated parallelization to try new configs on the fly.
5. It does not adapt to the data or allow for real-time adjustments based on evolving metrics.

RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach addresses these issues by providing real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, making the evaluation process more efficient and reliable.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 10379:
RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach with IC Ops avoids all the above issues,
while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in 
conjunction for even lower runtimes/costs.


Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and 
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 9430:
Note that apart from time, on closed model APIs, your token spend is also reallocated 
to more productive configs, which offers better return on investment for your use case.


Why Not Just Downsample?
------------------------

One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here. 
:doc:`As also explained on this page</difference>`, downsampling alone has 
significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI. 

First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence 
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually 
over and over, but that adds manual grunt work of juggling separate samples/files. 
Finally, downsampling alone does not offer you the power of IC Ops and automated 
parallelization to try new configs on the fly--you'd have reimplement those manually.

When using only closed model APIs such as OpenAI, RapidFire AI's scheduler automatically 
optimizes how CPU cores and the token rate limits are apportioned across configs. 
This will help avoid wastage of token spend on unproductive RAG configs and help you 
redirect the spend to more productive RAG configs in real time.


Why Not Just Downsample Data?
------------

At first glance, one might consider running multi-config comparisons by downsampling data for 
quick estimates, then running promising configs on full data. While common, this approach is 
often misleading and cumbersome.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 4884:
A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong 
conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone LLMs/DL models. It requires manual checkpoint 
management, adding tedious file work. You also do not get dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify),
or you must reimplement such tricky operations, taking time away from your AI application work.

RapidFire AI takes such practical heuristics to their logical conclusion with shard-based 
adaptive multi-config execution with dynamic experiment control. This offers you maximum power 
and flexibility for AI development without extra DevOps grunt work, i.e., *rapid experimentation*.

The above said, note that downsampling is *complementary* to rapid experimentation--feel free 
do both! The adaptive execution can operate on your downsampled dataset all the same.

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

ImportError in between Experiments
------

If you run multiple experiments back to back from the same notebook/IDE session, you might 
see the following error appear occasionally: 

.. code-block:: python

   ImportError: cannot import name 'GenerationMixin' from 'transformers.generation'

This is caused by stray Python processes from the previous experiment not ending properly. 
If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:

* Run the command :code:`ps - ef | grep python`, look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes, and kill if there are any with command :code:`kill -9 [PID]`.

* Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill as above.

* Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

API: Experiment 
================

Overview
--------

An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation. 

Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts. 
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

The Experiment class has the functions and semantics detailed below. 
As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either :code:`"fit"` mode or :code:`"eval"` mode but not both. 
We plan to allow both modes in the same experiment very soon.

.. note::
  Only one function in this class can be run at a time. If you interrupt a long-running function, 
  say, :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()`, wait for up to 2min for the Python threads to be 
  cleaned up before running another function.

RapidFire AI argues that simply downsampling the evaluation data is insufficient compared to its online aggregation approach because:

1. Downsampling requires deciding a sample size upfront, which is challenging when evaluation metrics have high variance across examples.
2. Point estimates without confidence intervals can give false confidence in a sample.
3. Manual resampling is tedious and requires juggling separate samples/files.
4. Downsampling alone does not offer the power of IC Ops and automated parallelization to try new configurations on the fly.
5. A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone models.
6. Downsampling requires manual checkpoint management, adding tedious file work.
7. Downsampling does not provide dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify) unless reimplemented manually.

RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach avoids these issues and is complementary to downsampling, allowing both to be used together for even lower runtimes and costs.

------------------------

One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here.

significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI. 

First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence 
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually 
over and over, but that adds manual grunt work of juggling separate samples/files. 
Finally, downsampling alone does not offer you the power of IC Ops and automated 
parallelization to try new configs on the fly--you'd have reimplement those manually.

while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in 
conjunction for even lower runtimes/costs.


Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and 
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 4884:
A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong 
conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone LLMs/DL models. It requires manual checkpoint 
management, adding tedious file work. You also do not get dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify),
or you must reimplement such tricky operations, taking time away from your AI application work.

RapidFire AI takes such practical heuristics to their logical conclusion with shard-based 
adaptive multi-config execution with dynamic experiment control. This offers you maximum power 
and flexibility for AI development without extra DevOps grunt work, i.e., *rapid experimentation*.

The above said, note that downsampling is *complementary* to rapid experimentation--feel free 
do both! The adaptive execution can operate on your downsampled dataset all the same.

.. image:: /images/gantt-2gpu.png
   :width: 800px

Likewise, for RAG/context engineering evals on self-hosted LLMs, the above multi-GPU 
scheduling optimizations also apply out of the box, albeit analogous to a single epoch. 
When using only closed model APIs such as OpenAI, RapidFire AI's scheduler automatically 
optimizes how CPU cores and the token rate limits are apportioned across configs. 
This will help avoid wastage of token spend on unproductive RAG configs and help you 
redirect the spend to more productive RAG configs in real time.


Why Not Just Downsample Data?
------------

At first glance, one might consider running multi-config comparisons by downsampling data for 
quick estimates, then running promising configs on full data. While common, this approach is 
often misleading and cumbersome.

Multi-GPU Model Support
------

Ordinarily, any given run's model(s) for its batch size must fit on a single GPU's memory. 
For DPO and GRPO, both the policy and reference models must fit on the GPU together. 

For SFT (and DPO), RapidFire AI can use FSDP automatically to partition a large model across GPUs on the same machine.
Provide the FSDP usage details in a config knob. See :doc:`the SFT page</sft>` FSDP section for more deatils.

To resolve an ImportError for GenerationMixin that occurs between experiments, follow these steps:

1. Run the command `ps -ef | grep python` to look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes.
2. Kill any identified processes with the command `kill -9 [PID]`.
3. Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill.
4. Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

This is caused by stray Python processes from the previous experiment not ending properly. 
If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:

* Run the command :code:`ps - ef | grep python`, look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes, and kill if there are any with command :code:`kill -9 [PID]`.

* Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill as above.

* Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

API: Experiment 
================

Overview
--------

An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation. 

Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts. 
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

The Experiment class has the functions and semantics detailed below. 
As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either :code:`"fit"` mode or :code:`"eval"` mode but not both. 
We plan to allow both modes in the same experiment very soon.

.. note::
  Only one function in this class can be run at a time. If you interrupt a long-running function, 
  say, :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()`, wait for up to 2min for the Python threads to be 
  cleaned up before running another function.


Experiment Constructor 
------

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 1779:
- .. figure:: /images/rag-eval-online2.png
          :width: 100%
          :alt: Online aggregation for evals with RapidFire AI and IC Ops.


All configs are executed on the first 1/8th of the data (50 examples), with 
their **incrementally computed** eval metrics shown in real time with confidence intervals. 
In the figure, the 3 worst configs are stopped, while the best is cloned to add 2 new variants. 
The 3 running configs now continue on the second 1/8th of the data (cumulatively, 
100 examples), and so on.
One clone is then stopped halfway through the aggregation, while the other two run to completion. 
Ultimately, the other clone ends up being the best config overall.

==============

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms your LLM pipeline customization 
from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, 
dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization.

For *RAG and context engineering evals*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: RAG and Context Engineering</walkthroughrag>`.

For *SFT and RFT/post-training workflows*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: SFT/RFT</walkthroughft>`.


RapidFire AI is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between the IDE
where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend.

.. image:: /images/rf-usage.png
   :width: 800px

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

Note that apart from time, on closed model APIs, your token spend is also reallocated

Why Not Just Downsample?
------------------------

One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here. 
:doc:`As also explained on this page</difference>`, downsampling alone has 
significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI. 

First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence 
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually 
over and over, but that adds manual grunt work of juggling separate samples/files. 
Finally, downsampling alone does not offer you the power of IC Ops and automated 
parallelization to try new configs on the fly--you'd have reimplement those manually.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

To resolve an ImportError for GenerationMixin that occurs between experiments, follow these steps:

1. Run the command `ps -ef | grep python` to identify any "multiprocessing.spawn" or "defunct" processes.
2. Kill any identified processes using the command `kill -9 [PID]`.
3. Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there were processes to kill.
4. Restart the kernel and proceed with your new experiment.

ImportError in between Experiments
------

If you run multiple experiments back to back from the same notebook/IDE session, you might 
see the following error appear occasionally: 

.. code-block:: python

   ImportError: cannot import name 'GenerationMixin' from 'transformers.generation'

This is caused by stray Python processes from the previous experiment not ending properly. 
If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:

* Run the command :code:`ps - ef | grep python`, look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes, and kill if there are any with command :code:`kill -9 [PID]`.

* Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill as above.

* Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

-------

We compare 2 generator models via OpenAI API: gpt-5-mini and gpt-4o.

=======================

Task, Dataset, and Prompt
-------

This tutorial shows Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for verifying scientific claims against evidence.

It uses the "SciFact" dataset from the BEIR benchmark; 
`see its details here <https://github.com/allenai/scifact>`__. 
The dataset contains scientific claims that must be labeled as SUPPORT, CONTRADICT, or NOINFO based on retrieved evidence.

API: LangChain RAG Spec
===============

RapidFire AI's core API for defining the stages of a RAG pipeline before the generator is a wrapper around the corresponding APIs of LangChain.
In particular, this class specifies all of the following stages: data loading, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, and reranking steps. 
Note that many of these stages are optional. 

Many of the arguments (knobs) here can also be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued depending 
on its data type, as explained below. All this forms the base set of knob combinations from which 
a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

Note that for plain prompt/context engineering use cases without RAG, you can skip providing this entire class. 
If you'd like to do few-shot prompting instead, also read :doc:`API: Prompt Manager and Other Eval Config Knobs page</promptothers>`.
Here is an illustration of the non-RAG prompt engineering workflow, with optional few-shot prompting.

The GSM8K tutorial configures its few-shot prompting pipeline using the RFPromptManager with the following settings:

- **Example Selection**: Semantic similarity-based selection using sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings.
- **Example Pool**: 10 hand-crafted examples.
- **Few-Shot k Values**: 2 values (3 and 5 examples per prompt).
- **Prompt Template**: Chain-of-thought style with step-by-step reasoning and final answer after "####".

The total number of config combinations produced is 6, calculated as 1 (generator) x 1 (reasoning effort level) x 2 (few-shot k values) + 1 (generator) x 2 (reasoning effort levels) x 2 (few-shot k values) = 6.

Task, Dataset, and Prompt
-------

This tutorial shows few-shot prompting as part of context engineering for solving grade school math word problems.

It uses the "GSM8K" dataset; 
`see its details here <https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k>`__. 
The dataset contains grade school math word problems requiring multi-step reasoning.

semantically selected few-shot examples, and the target question to solve.


Model, Few-Shot Selection, and Configuration Knobs
-------

We compare 2 generator models via OpenAI API: gpt-5-mini and gpt-4o.

There are 2 different reasoning effort levels for the first model only: medium and high.

The few-shot prompting pipeline uses:

- **Example Selection**: Semantic similarity-based selection using sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings.
- **Example Pool**: 10 hand-crafted examples covering diverse problem types.
- **Few-Shot k Values**: 2 different values: 3 and 5 examples per prompt.
- **Prompt Template**: Chain-of-thought style with step-by-step reasoning and final answer after "####".

API: Prompt Manager and Other Eval Config Knobs
===============

RFPromptManager
------

This class wraps around some LangChain APIs to manage dynamic few-shot example selection. It provides semantic 
similarity-based example selection to construct prompts with the most relevant examples for each input query.

The individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued in an :class:`RFPromptManager`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can be produced. 
Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

.. py:class:: RFPromptManager

  :param instructions: The main instructions for the prompt that guide the generator's behavior. This sets the overall task description and role for the assistant. Either this or :code:`instructions_file_path` must be provided.
  :type instructions: str, optional

To install and initialize RapidFire AI for fine-tuning workflows:

1. Install Python 3.12+ and create a virtual environment:
   ```bash
   python3 --version  # must be 3.12.x
   python3 -m venv .venv
   source .venv/bin/activate
   ```

2. Install RapidFire AI:
   ```bash
   pip install rapidfireai
   ```

3. Verify the installation:
   ```bash
   rapidfireai --version
   # Verify it prints: RapidFire AI 0.14.0
   ```

4. Initialize RapidFire AI server:
   ```bash
   rapidfireai init
   ```

To access gated Hugging Face models:

1. Install the Hugging Face Hub CLI:
   ```bash
   pip install "huggingface-hub[cli]"
   ```

2. Authenticate with your Hugging Face token:
   ```bash
   hf auth login --token YOUR_TOKEN
   ```

3. Uninstall hf-xet due to a known issue:
   ```bash
   pip uninstall -y hf-xet
   ```

--------------------

Optional user-provided function to postprocess a batch of examples and their respective generated outputs, 
which is injected into this function by the system. 
This is useful for, say, extracting structured information from generations, adding ground truth data,

API: User-Provided Functions for Run Evals
===============

Users can provide the following custom functions as part of their eval config to be used in :func:`run_evals()`.
Note that each leaf config can have its own set of functions for all of these.


Preprocess Function
-------------------

Mandatory user-provided function to prepare the inputs to be given to the generator model. 
It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process before generation.
Pass it directly to the :code:`preprocess_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.

The system injects into this function the batch data, as well as the RAG spec and 
the prompt manager of an individual leaf config.


.. py:function:: preprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list], rag: RFLangChainRagSpec, prompt_manager: RFPromptManager) -> dict[str, list]

   :param batch: Dictionary with a batch of examples with dataset field names as keys and lists as values
   :type batch: dict[str, list]

Other Eval Config Knobs
------

Finally, apart from the Generator, the following knobs can also be included in your eval config dictionary. Each of 
these can also be a knob set generator, viz., :func:`List()` for a discrete and :func:`Range()` for continuous knobs.

For more details on the four user-given functions listed below, see :doc:`the API: User-Provided Functions for Run Evals page</evalsfunctions>`.

For more details on the semantics of the online aggregation strategy arguments listed below, see :doc:`the Online Aggregation for Evals page</onlineagg>`.


**batch_size** : int
	Number of examples to process in one batch for GPU efficiency (if applicable)

RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach with IC Ops avoids all the above issues,
while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in 
conjunction for even lower runtimes/costs.


Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and 
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 9430:
Note that apart from time, on closed model APIs, your token spend is also reallocated 
to more productive configs, which offers better return on investment for your use case.


Why Not Just Downsample?
------------------------

One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here. 
:doc:`As also explained on this page</difference>`, downsampling alone has 
significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI. 

First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence 
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually 
over and over, but that adds manual grunt work of juggling separate samples/files. 
Finally, downsampling alone does not offer you the power of IC Ops and automated 
parallelization to try new configs on the fly--you'd have reimplement those manually.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

Known Issues and Updates Coming Soon
=============

As of this writing, RapidFire AI has the following known issues. We have listed some 
recommended recourses for some. 
We are actively working on resolving these and welcome feedback on their utility for your 
use cases to help with prioritization.


Multi-GPU Model Support
------

Ordinarily, any given run's model(s) for its batch size must fit on a single GPU's memory. 
For DPO and GRPO, both the policy and reference models must fit on the GPU together. 

For SFT (and DPO), RapidFire AI can use FSDP automatically to partition a large model across GPUs on the same machine.
Provide the FSDP usage details in a config knob. See :doc:`the SFT page</sft>` FSDP section for more deatils. 
Support for GRPO coming soon. 
We also plan to add support for multi-GPU model partitioning via DeepSpeed soon.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/issues.rst; start_index: -1:
ImportError in between Experiments
------

If you run multiple experiments back to back from the same notebook/IDE session, you might 
see the following error appear occasionally: 

.. code-block:: python

   ImportError: cannot import name 'GenerationMixin' from 'transformers.generation'

This is caused by stray Python processes from the previous experiment not ending properly. 
If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

RapidFire AI argues that simply downsampling the evaluation data is insufficient compared to its online aggregation approach because:

1. Downsampling requires deciding a sample size upfront, which is challenging if evaluation metrics have high variance across examples.
2. Point estimates without confidence intervals from downsampling can give false confidence in a sample.
3. Manual resampling adds extra work of juggling separate samples/files.
4. Downsampling alone does not provide the power of IC Ops and automated parallelization to try new configurations on the fly, which would need to be reimplemented manually.
5. RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach avoids these issues and is complementary to downsampling, allowing for even lower runtimes and costs when used together.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/difference.rst; start_index: 0:
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

To resolve an ImportError for GenerationMixin that occurs between experiments, follow these steps:

1. Run the command `ps -ef | grep python` to look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes.
2. Kill any such processes using the command `kill -9 [PID]`.
3. Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill.
4. Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

ImportError in between Experiments
------

If you run multiple experiments back to back from the same notebook/IDE session, you might 
see the following error appear occasionally: 

.. code-block:: python

   ImportError: cannot import name 'GenerationMixin' from 'transformers.generation'

This is caused by stray Python processes from the previous experiment not ending properly. 
If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:

* Run the command :code:`ps - ef | grep python`, look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes, and kill if there are any with command :code:`kill -9 [PID]`.

* Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill as above.

* Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

Glossary of Key Terms and Concepts
==========


Artifacts
-----
All files related to an experiment saved under in a local folder with its path specified by
:code:`experiments_path` in the experiment's constructor.
Includes the final (and possibly all epoch-level) model checkpoints of all runs across 
all :func:`run_fit()` in that experiment, and all associated metrics files.

Read more here: :doc:`API: Experiment</experiment>`.


Config Dictionary
-----

A dictionary of key-value pairs that specify a full model training configuration. 
A knob's value can be a singleton or set-valued (:class:`List` or :class:`Range`). 
A dictionary with set-valued knobs be fed to a config-group generator method. 
A single combination of knob values in this dictionary is called a "leaf" config. 
RapidFire AI instantiates one run per leaf config, and its values are injected via the 
:code:`model_config` argument to your :func:`create_model_fn()` function.

RapidFire AI's core API for defining the stages of a RAG pipeline before the generator is a wrapper around the corresponding APIs of LangChain.
In particular, this class specifies all of the following stages: data loading, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, and reranking steps.

a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

answer: RapidFire AI argues that simply downsampling the evaluation data is insufficient compared to its online aggregation approach because downsampling alone has significant disadvantages. These include the need to decide a downsample size upfront, which is challenging if eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence intervals can give false confidence in a sample. Additionally, downsampling does not offer the power of IC Ops and automated parallelization to try new configs on the fly, requiring manual reimplementation. RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach avoids these issues and is complementary to downsampling, allowing for even lower runtimes and costs.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 9430:
Note that apart from time, on closed model APIs, your token spend is also reallocated 
to more productive configs, which offers better return on investment for your use case.


Why Not Just Downsample?
------------------------

One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here. 
:doc:`As also explained on this page</difference>`, downsampling alone has 
significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI. 

First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence 
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually 
over and over, but that adds manual grunt work of juggling separate samples/files. 
Finally, downsampling alone does not offer you the power of IC Ops and automated 
parallelization to try new configs on the fly--you'd have reimplement those manually.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 10379:
RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach with IC Ops avoids all the above issues,
while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in 
conjunction for even lower runtimes/costs.


Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and 
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.

source: sourcedocs/sourcedocs/onlineagg.rst; start_index: 0:
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

To resolve an ImportError for GenerationMixin that occurs between experiments, follow these steps:

1. Run the command `ps -ef | grep python` to look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes.
2. Kill any such processes with the command `kill -9 [PID]`.
3. Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill.
4. Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

------

see the following error appear occasionally:

RFSFTConfig
------

This is a wrapper around :class:`SFTConfig` in HF TRL. 
The full signature and list of arguments are available on `this page 
<https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/sft_trainer#trl.SFTConfig>`__.

The only difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued 
or :class:`Range` valued in :class:`RFSFTConfig`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can be 
produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.
Other than the multi-config specification, this class preserves all semantics of Hugging Face's 
SFT trainer under the hood.

Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and 
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.
